Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space. A measurable function
$s:X\to[0,+\infty)\subseteq\overline{\mathbb R}$
([[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]) is a
**nonnegative simple measurable function** when it has finite range.

Equivalently, there are pairwise disjoint measurable sets
$E_1,\dots,E_m\in\mathcal A$ and coefficients $c_1,\dots,c_m\in[0,+\infty)$
such that
$$s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}.$$
Any such display is a **simple representation** of $s$.

Let $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\chi_{E_j}$ be a simple representation of a
nonnegative simple measurable function
([[def-nonnegative-simple-measurable-function]]) on a measure space
$(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$, so the $E_j\in\mathcal A$ are pairwise disjoint and
$c_j\ge0$. Its
**simple integral** is
$$\int s\,d\mu:=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mu(E_j),$$
where $\mu$ is the given measure ([[def-measure]]) and the convention
$0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ is fixed once and for all.

The next lemma proves that this value is independent of the chosen simple
representation.

If $s$ is a nonnegative simple measurable function, then its nonnegative
Lebesgue integral equals its simple integral:
$$\int s\,d\mu=\int_{\mathrm{simple}} s\,d\mu.$$

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: If $s=\sum_{j=1}^m c_j\mathbf 1_{A_j}$ is a nonnegative simple function with pairwise disjoint $A_j\in\mathcal A$, then [F1] and [F2] give $\int s\,d\delta_{x_0}=\sum_jc_j\delta_{x_0}(A_j)=\sum_jc_j\mathbf 1_{A_j}(x_0)=s(x_0)$.

Choose the increasing simple approximation $s_n\uparrow f$ from [F3]. By [F4] and step 1.1, $\int f\,d\delta_{x_0}=\lim_n\int s_n\,d\delta_{x_0}=\lim_ns_n(x_0)=f(x_0)$, including when the value is $+\infty$.

boundaries.reason: The hypotheses include a point x0 in X, so X is nonempty.

boundaries.evidence: For f=0 the identity is step 1.1–2.1 and both sides are zero.
For f=1 the Dirac mass has total mass one by step 1.1–2.1.
The point mass is the degenerate measure; step 1.1 evaluates every simple function at x0.
If f(x0)=+infinity, the monotone limit in step 2.1 retains +infinity.
The explicit simple approximation in step 2.1 uses no arbitrary-family choice.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

derivations.claim: For each $x\in\mathcal X$, the section $B\mapsto K_T(x,B)=\delta_{T(x)}(B)$ is the probability measure $\delta_{T(x)}$ by [F2].

For each $B\in\mathcal G$, $x\mapsto K_T(x,B)=\mathbf 1_B(T(x))=\mathbf 1_{T^{-1}(B)}(x)$ is $\mathcal A$-measurable by [F1]. Thus both clauses of the kernel definition [F3] hold, so $K_T$ is a probability kernel, hence a deterministic randomized procedure.

For B=empty, every event evaluation is zero by step 1.1.
For B equal to the action space, every section has mass one by step 1.1.
A constant statistic gives a constant Dirac kernel; steps 1.1 and 2.1 still apply.

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment: a measurable data space, a parameter-label set,
and a family of probability measures on the data space. Let
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be its real-valued target function (estimand). An estimator
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is a measurable statistic
with the real Borel target ([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]). At a parameter
$\theta$ for which $T$ is integrable under $P_\theta$, its **bias** is
$$\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[T]-\psi(\theta).$$

Its **mean squared error** (MSE) is the extended nonnegative number
$$\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\psi(\theta))^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
This is the risk of the deterministic rule induced by $T$ under squared-error
loss $L(\theta,a)=(a-\psi(\theta))^2$: its Dirac kernel is constructed in
[[lem-statistic-induces-deterministic-procedure]], and the risk supplier's
integral formula reduces to the displayed expectation when the action is
$T(x)$ by [[lem-dirac-integral-evaluation]]
([[def-loss-function-and-risk]]). For each fixed $\theta$, this loss is Borel
in the real action $a$; no measurable structure on $\Theta$ or measurability
of $\psi$ is required. The expectation convention is
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. If $T$ is
square-integrable under $P_\theta$, then its variance is defined by
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and this MSE is finite. Bias is not
defined at parameters where $T$ is not integrable.

Let $X$ be a real random variable on a probability space.

- For $p>0$, the **$p$th absolute moment** of $X$ exists when $|X|^p$ is
  integrable, and is then
  $$\mathbb E[|X|^p].$$
- If $X$ is integrable, its **mean** is $\mathbb E[X]$.
- If $X$ is square-integrable, its **variance** is
  $$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2].$$

If $X$ and $Y$ are square-integrable real random variables on the same
probability space, their **covariance** is
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

derivations.claim: Fix $\theta$, put $\mu=\mathbb E_\theta[T]$ and $b=\mu-\psi(\theta)$. Square-integrability makes $T$ integrable, and [F1] gives $b=\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)$ while $T-\psi(\theta)=(T-\mu)+b$.

Expanding the square and using $\mathbb E_\theta[T-\mu]=0$ by [F3] gives $\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T)=\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\mu)^2]+b^2=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)+\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)^2$ by [F1] and [F2].

When bias is zero, step 2.1 reduces MSE to variance.
For a constant estimator, step 2.1 gives zero variance and MSE equal to squared bias.
If T is almost surely constant, the centered term in step 2.1 vanishes.

boundaries.evidence: The expansion in steps 1.1 and 2.1 is choice-free.

Let $T$ be an estimator of a real estimand $\psi$ in a statistical experiment.
It is **unbiased** if it is integrable under every $P_\theta$ and
$$\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.$$
Equivalently, its bias from [[def-bias-and-mean-squared-error]] is zero at every
parameter. It is a **finite-variance unbiased estimator** if it is unbiased
and square-integrable under every $P_\theta$.

A finite-variance unbiased estimator $T$ is **uniformly minimum-variance
unbiased** (UMVU) for $\psi$ if, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and every other
finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$ of the same estimand,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U).$$
The same estimator must satisfy these inequalities throughout the parameter
space; the definition asserts no existence of a UMVU estimator. Variance has
the meaning in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Standard Borelness ensures individual regular conditional distributions exist by [[thm-existence-of-regular-conditional-distributions-for-standard-borel-targets]]; sufficiency additionally asks that versions agree across parameters.

Let $K$ be a randomized procedure for the experiment
$\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
with action space $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$. Give $[0,+\infty]$ its Borel
sigma-algebra. For every nonnegative $\mathcal G/\mathcal B([0,+\infty])$-
measurable function $g:\mathsf D\to[0,+\infty]$, the function
$$h_g(x)=\int_{\mathsf D}g(a)\,K(x,da)$$
is $\mathcal A$-measurable. In particular, $x\mapsto K(x,B)$ is measurable
for every action event $B\in\mathcal G$. For each $\theta\in\Theta$, the
set function
$$Q_\theta(B)=\int_{\mathcal X}K(x,B)\,P_\theta(dx),\qquad B\in\mathcal G,$$
is a probability measure on $(\mathsf D,\mathcal G)$, and for every such $g$,
$$\int_{\mathsf D}g\,dQ_\theta=\int_{\mathcal X}\left(\int_{\mathsf D}g(a)\,K(x,da)\right)P_\theta(dx).$$
with nonnegative extended values allowed.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

1. If $f,g:X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$ are measurable and $f+g$ is defined
   pointwise, then $f+g$ is measurable.
2. If $c\in\mathbb R$ and $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $cf$ is
   measurable.
3. If $f:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, then $f^+=\max\{f,0\}$,
   $f^-=\max\{-f,0\}$, and $|f|=f^++f^-$ are measurable.
4. If $E\in\mathcal A$ and $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, then
   $f\chi_E$ is measurable, where this function equals $f$ on $E$ and $0$
   off $E$ (in particular, $0\cdot(+\infty)=0$ here).
5. If $(f_n)$ is a sequence of measurable functions $X\to\overline{\mathbb R}$,
   then $\inf_n f_n$ is measurable; if moreover $f_n\uparrow f$ pointwise, then
   $f$ is measurable.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then there is an increasing sequence of
nonnegative simple measurable functions $(s_n)$ such that $s_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x\in X$.

Let $0\le f_1\le f_2\le\cdots$ be measurable and suppose $f_n(x)\uparrow f(x)$
for every $x$. Then
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $f : X \to Y$ be a function and assume the target $Y$ carries a Borel
sigma-algebra $\mathcal{B}(Y)$.

The **sigma-algebra generated by $f$** is

$$\sigma(f) := \{\, f^{-1}(B) : B \in \mathcal{B}(Y) \,\}.$$

Because preimages preserve complements and countable unions, this is a
sigma-algebra on $X$. It is the smallest sigma-algebra on $X$ that makes $f$
measurable.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space, $\mathcal G\subseteq\mathcal F$ a sub-sigma-algebra, and $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ integrable. A **conditional-expectation version of $X$ given $\mathcal G$** is a real, $\mathcal G$-measurable, integrable function $Y$ such that $\int_A Y\,dP=\int_A X\,dP$ for every $A\in\mathcal G$. No completeness of $\mathcal G$ is assumed.

Expectation means the integral of [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. Integrable representatives use [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]]; quotient notation is introduced after uniqueness.

Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.
Assume AC. For $1\le p\le\infty$, conditional expectation is a linear map from real $L^p(P)$ to real $L^p(P|_{\mathcal G})$ satisfying $\|E[X\mid\mathcal G]\|_p\le\|X\|_p$.

Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.

Assume AC. Real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ embeds isometrically as a closed subspace of real $L^2(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$. For $X\in L^2(P)$, $U=E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ is its orthogonal projection onto this subspace. It uniquely minimizes $E[(X-Z)^2]$ over $Z\in L^2(\mathcal G)$ as an almost-sure class.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. Then
$$\int f\,d\mu=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad f=0 \text{ almost everywhere.}$$

derivations.claim: Write $u$ for the measurable function defining $U$. By [F2] and [F3], $h_+(s)=\int u^+dK(s,\cdot)$, $h_-(s)=\int u^-dK(s,\cdot)$, and $r(s)=\int|u|dK(s,\cdot)$ are Borel. Let $g=h_+-h_-$ where $r<\infty$ and $g=0$ elsewhere; [F6] makes both terms finite on this Borel set, and [F3] makes $g$ Borel.

Fix $\theta$ and a Borel statistic event $B$. For nonnegative simple functions of the data, [L1] and finite linearity give $\int_B\int s(x)K(t,dx)P_\theta^S(dt)=\mathbb E_\theta[\mathbf1_{\{S\in B\}}s(X)]$. Approximate $u^+$ and $u^-$ increasingly by simple functions using [F4]; [F5] passes each equality to the limit. Applying the same identity to $|u|$ with $B=\mathsf S$ gives $\mathbb E_\theta r(S)=\mathbb E_\theta|U|<\infty$. If $N=\{r(S)=+\infty\}$ had positive probability, then $m\mathbf1_N\leq r(S)$ for every positive integer $m$, so [F6] would give $mP_\theta(N)\leq\mathbb E_\theta r(S)$ for all $m$, a contradiction; thus $r(S)<\infty$ almost surely. The two finite event-integral identities may therefore be subtracted, giving $\mathbb E_\theta[\mathbf1_{\{S\in B\}}g(S)]=\mathbb E_\theta[\mathbf1_{\{S\in B\}}U]$. By [F7], [F8], and [F9], $g(S)$ is a version of $\mathbb E_\theta[U\mid\sigma(S)]$ as an almost-sure class for every $\theta$.
By [F10], $g(S)$ is square-integrable under each $P_\theta$. By [F11], $\mathbb E_\theta[g(S)]=\mathbb E_\theta[U]=\psi(\theta)$; hence it is an unbiased finite-variance estimator.

Fix $\theta$. The residual $U-g(S)$ is orthogonal in $L^2(P_\theta)$ to every square-integrable $\sigma(S)$-measurable function by [F12]. Since $g(S)-\psi(\theta)$ is such a function, expanding the centered square gives $\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U)=\mathbb E_\theta[(U-g(S))^2]+\operatorname{Var}_\theta(g(S))$. The first term is nonnegative, proving the variance inequality.

By [F14], equality in step 4.1 holds exactly when $U=g(S)$ $P_\theta$-almost surely. Since $g(S)$ is $\sigma(S)$-measurable, this is precisely almost-sure $\sigma(S)$-measurability: if $U$ has such a representative, its $L^2$ class lies in the projection subspace and [F12] fixes it.

boundaries.evidence: Statement: all conclusions are quantified over theta and are vacuous for an empty parameter set.
For U=0 and psi=0, the construction in step 1.1 gives g=0 and step 4.1 has zero residual.
For a constant-one estimator with target one, the conditional mean is one and step 5.1 gives equality.
For degenerate sampling laws, the event identities in step 2.1 and L2 equality in step 4.1 remain valid.

boundaries.reason: No scalar endpoint restriction is imposed; Bernoulli endpoints are checked on the B page.

boundaries.evidence: AC is stated and used through the conditional-expectation/L2 suppliers in steps 1.1–5.1; the common kernel is supplied.
Equality of variances implies U=g(S) almost surely by step 5.1.
If U is sigma(S)-measurable, the projection property in step 5.1 fixes its L2 class and gives equality.

axiom_uses.reason: Conditional-expectation existence and L2 projection assume AC; the common RCD is supplied as a sufficiency hypothesis, and finite Bernoulli arithmetic is choice-free.

Let $T$ be an estimator of a real estimand $\psi$ in a statistical experiment.
It is **unbiased** if it is integrable under every $P_\theta$ and
$$\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.$$
Equivalently, its bias from [[def-bias-and-mean-squared-error]] is zero at every
parameter. It is a **finite-variance unbiased estimator** if it is unbiased
and square-integrable under every $P_\theta$.

A finite-variance unbiased estimator $T$ is **uniformly minimum-variance
unbiased** (UMVU) for $\psi$ if, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and every other
finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$ of the same estimand,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U).$$
The same estimator must satisfy these inequalities throughout the parameter
space; the definition asserts no existence of a UMVU estimator. Variance has
the meaning in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the library conditional-expectation
convention. Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ have
standard-Borel data space, let $\mathsf S$ be standard Borel, and let
$S:\mathcal X\to\mathsf S$ be a sufficient statistic. Here sufficiency uses
a **supplied common kernel** $K(s,\cdot)$ that is a regular conditional law of
the data given $S=s$ under every $P_\theta$ and does not depend on $\theta$
([[def-sufficient-statistic]]). For Borel $B\subseteq\mathsf S$, write $P_\theta^S(B):=P_\theta(S^{-1}(B))$ for the pushforward law of $S$. Let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and let $U$ be
a measurable real estimator with $\mathbb E_\theta[U]=\psi(\theta)$ and
$\mathbb E_\theta[U^2]<\infty$ for every $\theta$.

There is a single Borel function $g:\mathsf S\to\mathbb R$, independent of
$\theta$, such that $g(S)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E_\theta[U\mid\sigma(S)]$ for every $\theta$. It is unbiased,
finite-variance, and
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(g(S))\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
For each $\theta$, equality holds exactly when $U$ is
$\sigma(S)$-measurable $P_\theta$-almost surely.

Let $((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta))$ be a statistical experiment, where $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ is standard Borel, and let $T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ be a statistic with standard Borel target. Write $P_\theta^T=P_\theta\circ T^{-1}$. The statistic $T$ is **sufficient** if there is one probability kernel $K$ from $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ to $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ such that, for every $\theta\in\Theta$, $A\in\mathcal A$, and $C\in\mathcal B$,

$$P_\theta(A\cap T^{-1}(C))=\int_C K(y,A)\,P_\theta^T(dy).$$

Thus $K(T(x),A)$ is a common version of the conditional probability of $A$ given $T$, under every parameter. The kernel is fixed independently of $\theta$. Let $T$ be an estimator of a real estimand $\psi$ in a statistical experiment.
It is **unbiased** if it is integrable under every $P_\theta$ and
$$\mathbb E_\theta[T]=\psi(\theta)\qquad\text{for every }\theta\in\Theta.$$
Equivalently, its bias from [[def-bias-and-mean-squared-error]] is zero at every
parameter. It is a **finite-variance unbiased estimator** if it is unbiased
and square-integrable under every $P_\theta$.

A finite-variance unbiased estimator $T$ is **uniformly minimum-variance
unbiased** (UMVU) for $\psi$ if, for every $\theta\in\Theta$ and every other
finite-variance unbiased estimator $U$ of the same estimand,
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U).$$
The same estimator must satisfy these inequalities throughout the parameter
space; the definition asserts no existence of a UMVU estimator. Variance has
the meaning in [[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]].

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment: a measurable data space, a parameter-label set,
and a family of probability measures on the data space. Let
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ be its real-valued target function (estimand). An estimator
$T:\mathcal X\to\mathbb R$ is a measurable statistic
with the real Borel target ([[def-statistic-and-estimator]]). At a parameter
$\theta$ for which $T$ is integrable under $P_\theta$, its **bias** is
$$\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[T]-\psi(\theta).$$

Its **mean squared error** (MSE) is the extended nonnegative number
$$\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T):=\mathbb E_\theta[(T-\psi(\theta))^2]\in[0,+\infty].$$
This is the risk of the deterministic rule induced by $T$ under squared-error
loss $L(\theta,a)=(a-\psi(\theta))^2$: its Dirac kernel is constructed in
[[lem-statistic-induces-deterministic-procedure]], and the risk supplier's
integral formula reduces to the displayed expectation when the action is
$T(x)$ by [[lem-dirac-integral-evaluation]]
([[def-loss-function-and-risk]]). For each fixed $\theta$, this loss is Borel
in the real action $a$; no measurable structure on $\Theta$ or measurability
of $\psi$ is required. The expectation convention is
[[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]]. If $T$ is
square-integrable under $P_\theta$, then its variance is defined by
[[def-moments-variance-and-covariance]] and this MSE is finite. Bias is not
defined at parameters where $T$ is not integrable.

For a finite family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$,
$$\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\sum_{i\in I}X_i\right)=\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{Var}(X_i)+2\sum_{\{i,j\}\subseteq I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j).$$
Equivalently, it is $\sum_{i,j\in I}\operatorname{Cov}(X_i,X_j)$. The empty sum has variance zero, and the singleton formula is the identity.
In the first display, the second sum is over two-element subsets of $I$.

If $X$ and $Y$ are independent square-integrable real random variables, then
$$\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0.$$

Thus independence implies zero covariance. The converse is false in general.

For real random variables $X$ and $Y$ on one finite probability space, define
$$\operatorname{Var}(X):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])^2],\qquad \operatorname{Cov}(X,Y):=\mathbb E[(X-\mathbb E[X])(Y-\mathbb E[Y])].$$
The **standard deviation** of $X$ is $\sigma_X:=\operatorname{Var}(X)^{1/2}$, using the unique nonnegative square root supplied by [[thm-of-square-roots]]. Variance is nonnegative because its defining random variable is pointwise nonnegative and expectation is a sum with nonnegative weights.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

In a statistical experiment, let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and let $T$ be a
real estimator with $\mathbb E_\theta[T^2]<\infty$. For every $\theta$,
$$\operatorname{MSE}_\theta(T)=\operatorname{Var}_\theta(T)+\operatorname{Bias}_\theta(T)^2.$$

Let $\mathsf E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be an experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). A **statistic** with target
measurable space $(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$ is a measurable map
$T:(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)\to(\mathcal Y,\mathcal B)$, where measurability
means that $T^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal A$ for every $B\in\mathcal B$
([[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]). If
$\psi:\Theta\to\mathcal Y$ is an estimand ([[def-estimand-on-a-statistical-model]])
and its target set $\mathcal Y$ is equipped with $\mathcal B$, a statistic
$\widehat\psi$ with this same target space is an **estimator of $\psi$**.
The value $\widehat\psi(x)$ is the estimate at observed data $x$. Giving
$\mathcal Y$ a measurable structure is an additional choice; this definition
does not assert that $\psi$ is measurable as a function of the parameter.

For $p\in[0,1]$, a **Bernoulli$(p)$ random variable** takes the value $1$ with probability $p$ and $0$ with probability $1-p$.

For $n\in\mathbb N$, a **binomial$(n,p)$ random variable** is a sum $X=\sum_{i<n}X_i$ of $n$ mutually independent Bernoulli$(p)$ variables. When $n=0$, this is the constant zero random variable.

A finite family of finite-valued random variables $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **mutually independent** when for every nonempty $J\subseteq I$ and every selection $x_j\in X_j(\Omega)$,
$$\mathbb P(X_j=x_j\text{ for every }j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\mathbb P(X_j=x_j).$$
It is **pairwise independent** when this identity is required only for two distinct indices. The empty family is mutually independent vacuously, and a one-member family is mutually independent.

derivations.claim: Each $X_i$ and $\overline X$ is measurable on the finite product space, hence an estimator by [F7]. The Bernoulli law [F8] gives $P_p(X_i=1)=p$ and $P_p(X_i=0)=1-p$; summing these two values gives $\mathbb E_pX_i=p$ and $\operatorname{Var}_p(X_i)=(1-p)p^2+p(1-p)^2=p(1-p)$, including $p=0,1$. Thus [F5] gives $\mathbb E_p\overline X=p$, so $\overline X$ is unbiased by [F1].

The independent $X_i$ are square-integrable, so [F3] makes every off-diagonal covariance zero. Applying [F2] gives $\operatorname{Var}_p(\sum_iX_i)=np(1-p)$ and hence $\operatorname{Var}_p(\overline X)=p(1-p)/n$. Since the bias is zero, [F6] gives the same value for MSE.

([[def-sufficient-statistic]]). For Borel $B\subseteq\mathsf S$, write $P_\theta^S(B):=P_\theta(S^{-1}(B))$ for the pushforward law of $S$. Let $\psi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$ and let $U$ be
a measurable real estimator with $\mathbb E_\theta[U]=\psi(\theta)$ and
$\mathbb E_\theta[U^2]<\infty$ for every $\theta$.

$\theta$, such that $g(S)$ is a version of
$\mathbb E_\theta[U\mid\sigma(S)]$ for every $\theta$. It is unbiased,
finite-variance, and
$$\operatorname{Var}_\theta(g(S))\leq\operatorname{Var}_\theta(U)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta).$$
For each $\theta$, equality holds exactly when $U$ is
$\sigma(S)$-measurable $P_\theta$-almost surely.

derivations.claim: For $s\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$ let $F_s=\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:\sum_i x_i=s\}$; it has $\binom ns\geq1$ elements. Define $K(s,A)=|A\cap F_s|/\binom ns$ for every data event $A$. This is a probability kernel independent of $p$. By [F4], independence makes the joint law the product of the Bernoulli coordinate masses. For $0<p<1$, each vector in $F_s$ therefore has the same mass $p^s(1-p)^{n-s}$, so $K(s,\cdot)$ is the conditional law given $S=s$. At $p=0$ or $p=1$, the only supported fibers are the singleton all-zero or all-one fiber, where the same kernel is the conditional law. Hence $K$ is a common regular conditional law and proves sufficiency by [L1].

For $0<p<1$, the uniform fiber law is invariant under coordinate permutations, so the $n$ conditional means $\mathbb E_p[X_i\mid S=s]$ agree. Their sum is $s$, hence each is $s/n$. At $p=0,1$, $X_1=S/n$ almost surely, so the same formula holds on the support. Also $\mathbb E_pX_1=p$, so [F2] and [F1] identify $S/n$ as the Rao–Blackwellized unbiased estimator; [F3] records its conditional-expectation class convention.
